Fragmenta in Lamentationes
1 Ὁ Ἱερεμίας αἰχμαλωτισθέντος τοῦ λαοῦ καὶ ὄντος ἐν Βαβυλῶνι, θρηνεῖ τὴν πόλιν
καὶ τὴν χώραν καὶ τὸν λαὸν ἐπὶ τοῖς συμβεβηκόσι, καὶ θρηνεῖ περικοπάς τινας καὶ
διαστολὰς περιγράφων ἀρχομένας ἑξῆς ἀπὸ τῶν παρ' Ἑβραίοις στοιχείων. καὶ μετὰ
τὸ τε λέσαι τὸν ἐφ' ἑκάστου στοιχείου Θρῆνον καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσι τὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ Θαῦ
ἀρχόμενον, ὅπερ ἐστὶ τελευταῖον τῶν Ἑβραίων γράμμα, ἐπανέρχεται ἐπὶ τὸ Ἄλφ καὶ
πάλιν θρηνεῖ, καὶ τοῦτο ποιεῖ τετράκις τὰ εἴκοσι καὶ δύο στοιχεῖα ἐπεξιών. 2 Ἐὰν
ἴδωμεν ὑποχείριον γινομένην τὴν ψυχὴν τῷ διαβόλῳ ἢ καὶ τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτοῦ, καὶ
ἁπαξαπλῶς ταῖς ἐχθραῖς δυνάμεσι τὴν τῇ φύσει θεωρητικὴν καὶ συνορᾶν τὰ ὄντα
<καὶ> ἐπιστῆσαι δυναμένην, νοήσομέν πως τὴν αἰχμαλωσίαν καὶ τὸν
αἰχμαλωτίσαντα . ἀλλὰ καταφυγόντες ἐπὶ τὸν Χριστόν, τὸν κηρύξαντα κατὰ τὸν
προφήτην Ἡσαΐαν «αἰχμαλώτοις ἄφεσιν», ἐλευθερωθησόμεθα ἀπὸ τῆς αἰχμα
λωσίας, κἂν μέχρι τοῦ δῆσαι φθάσῃ ὁ αἰ

Jeremiah, seeing his people captive in Babylon, grieves for the city, land, and people because of what happened. He mourns specific parts and sections, marking them in order, starting from the Hebrew basic elements and going forward. After writing a lament for each element alone, and then one for all things beginning with Tau—the last Hebrew letter—he goes back to Aleph and laments again. He does this four times, covering the twenty-two elements.

If we see the soul given over to the devil or his angels, and simply surrendering to enemy forces, thus losing the mind’s power to contemplate and perceive reality, we will somehow grasp what captivity and the captor mean. But by taking refuge in Christ, who announced, per Isaiah, “Freedom for captives,” we will be freed from captivity, even if the captor ties us up before freedom comes. For Jesus came “to release those bound in chains, and those sitting in darkness in prison.”

Thus, the Hebrews claim the books of the old Scripture match the number of elements, to provide full access to knowing God, just as elements introduce wisdom to learners. Hence the number is multiplied by four, maybe because bodily elements are four. Soon after: Aquila and Theodotion’s version is absent from the Lamentations; only Symmachus and the Seventy appear. Again: One may ask how the book’s title is plural—“Lamentations”—yet the prologue uses singular “Lamentation.” But some manuscripts show many variants, split by elements, while all converge into one, toward a single idea: Israel, as they are remembered.

Blessed is the tear from love, since the holy says, “Weep with those who weep.” As the Lord approached Jerusalem, he wept and said: “If you, even you, had known today what makes for peace.” Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you slay prophets and stone the messengers—how often I wished to gather your young like a hen broods her chicks beneath her wings, yet you refused. Since “blessed are the weepers, for they shall laugh,” Jeremiah the mystic ought to have wept this lament and, per “blessed are the mourners,” mourned those deserving of grief. The crowd of the people, as spoken, means the Israelites residing; the crowd of nations, as noted, means the converts. For uplift, since theory is soul-like and steadfast over practice, the people’s multitude may denote Jerusalem’s blessed store of doctrines; the nations’ multitude, the many good deeds. Soon: The people-filled alone sits; the bride, having rejected the groom’s word, grows like a widow who once increased among the named nations. By the letter, Jerusalem should be thought spoken of in wonder, due to her shift to the grim, having sat recalling the people who once were many, so her loneliness and waste be hers—having had a husband, the living guardian, when she followed him present and aiding, now abandoned by him for her faults. pass_b_english:
Jeremiah, after his people had been taken captive and were dwelling in Babylon, laments the city, the land, and the people in light of the events that have befallen them. He mourns particular sections and divisions, tracing them in writing, beginning with the elementary elements as known among the Hebrews, and proceeding sequentially. After composing a lament for each of these elements individually, and then a lament over all things beginning with the letter Tau—which is the final letter of the Hebrew alphabet—he returns to Aleph and laments again. He repeats this process four times, going through the twenty-two elements of the Hebrew alphabet.

If we observe the soul becoming subject to the devil, or even to his angels, and simply yielding to the hostile powers, thereby losing the capacity for intellectual contemplation and the ability to perceive and understand being, we shall in some way comprehend the nature of captivity and the one who has taken captive. Yet, by fleeing to Christ, who proclaimed, according to the prophet Isaiah, “Release to the captives,” we shall be set free from captivity, even if the captor manages to bind us before liberation arrives. For Jesus came “to bring out those bound in chains, and those sitting in darkness in the house of prison.”

Therefore, the Hebrews say that the books of the ancient Scripture correspond in number to the elements, so as to constitute a complete introduction to the knowledge of God, just as the elements serve as an introduction to wisdom for all who learn. And for this reason, the number is quadrupled, perhaps because the elements of the body are four in number. Shortly thereafter: The edition of Aquila and Theodotion is not found among the Lamentations; only that of Symmachus and the Seventy is present. Again: One might inquire how, given that the superscription of the book is plural—“Lamentations”—the singular “Lamentation” appears in the prologue. But some manuscripts have multiple readings, divided according to the elements, while all are ultimately brought back to one, toward a single hypothesis: Israel, as they are recalled.

Blessed is the tear shed from love, for the holy one says, “Weep with those who weep.” As the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, he wept and said: “If you, even you, had only known on this day what would bring you peace.”

Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you—how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing. Now if “blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh,” then it was fitting that Jeremiah, this mystic one, should weep a weeping of mourning and, according to “blessed are those who mourn,” should mourn those worthy of mourning. It seems, however, that the multitude of the people, insofar as it is spoken of, denotes the Israelites dwelling there, while the multitude of the nations, as we have said before, denotes the proselytes. For the purpose of uplift, since the theoretical things are more akin to the soul and more constant than the practical, the multitude of the people might signify the wealth of the doctrines of the blessed Jerusalem, and the multitude of the nations the great number of good works. And shortly after: The people, filled alone, sits; the bride, having cast away the bridegroom’s word, becomes like a widow who once multiplied among the aforesaid nations. As far as the words go, it is fitting to understand Jerusalem as being spoken of with wonder, due to her change toward the more grim, having sat down remembering the people who once were numerous, so that her solitude and desolation might be hers—having once had a husband, the vivifying preserver, when she followed him present and helping, and now being deserted and forsaken by him on account of her sins. And furthermore: These things, then, pertain to the literal sense; but for the intellectual sense, Jerusalem, enriching herself and multiplying among peoples and nations and ruling over regions, is the divine soul. And it is not marvelous, if not only a house, nor even a homestead, nor even this village, if it were called such, nor even the city that possesses such things, but rather Jerusalem, surpassing all cities and honored by God, is named the perfect soul—of a magnitude worthy of a great city, by the greatest surrounding that envelops it from
